source: Pease (2007) A Computational Model of Lakatos-style Reasoning (PhD thesis, Edinburgh), ch. 10 setup
finding: The evaluation of the HRL system (HR extended with Lakatos methods) tests only whether changing parameters changes output. It does not compare against a baseline system. Three hypotheses: the methods of surrender, monster-barring and exception-barring can each be fine-tuned. Domains: group theory, animal taxonomy, number theory. Monster-adjusting was left unimplemented.
numbers: Sessions numbered 1-92; 3 domains; results judged by the students' own interestingness score (threshold 0.8) or by the author's list of expected monsters.
limits: No control arm, no human-rated outcomes, small counts. The author says the number of modifications was too low to draw conclusions on optimal settings.
agent_relevance: There is no measured evidence that Lakatos-style repair beats plain resampling. Our question (c) in SUBFIELDS has no prior answer from this model; we must run it ourselves at equal tokens.

source: Pease (2007) thesis, section 10.3 (method of surrender)
finding: Best setting for surrender was the plain default: drop any conjecture that has a counterexample (number-of-modifications = 0). It was one of the best indicators of all variables tested. Setting modifications to 3 was worst: it modified every conjecture, most of which the students rated uninteresting.
numbers: Modification limit 0 best; limit 3 gave only quadrant (ii)/(iii) conjectures (the ones to minimise) in every domain. Only the animal taxonomy students found conjectures worth modifying.
limits: Interestingness is the system's own measure. The author says the interestingness settings themselves should be changed in future runs.
agent_relevance: Repairing everything is worse than dropping a claim. Supports a cap on repair attempts per claim and a rule that cheap claims are discarded rather than patched (fits G7, G12).

source: Pease (2007) thesis, section 10.4 (monster-barring)
finding: Monster-barring worked best with the plain Lakatos rule (propose to bar any counterexample object of the claim under discussion) or a low threshold (up to 30-40 percent). Stricter 'culprit breaker' rules (an object makes more than half the theory into counterexamples) were too strict and found no monsters. In number theory the system first missed 0 and 1 as monsters because the one student set to bar never met them in a counterexample. Making all students able to bar fixed this; the best session barred both 0 and 1 with a 10 percent minimum.
numbers: Sessions 1-24 and 69-92. Number theory scored 97 percent correct only because the 2 expected monsters were missed and nearly all other objects were correctly left alone. Platypus found as the only monster in animal theory in sessions 69, 71, 74. Author hypothesis: a 10 percent barring minimum is best.
limits: Gold list of monsters was chosen by the author. Accuracy percentage is inflated by true negatives. Sessions timed out before some counterexamples appeared.
agent_relevance: A classification score must report recall on the rare case, not overall accuracy. Whether an object is a monster depends on which counterexamples the run happened to meet, so code should enumerate counterexamples before classifying (SUBFIELDS question a).

source: Pease (2007) thesis, section 10.5 (exception-barring: piecemeal exclusion, strategic withdrawal)
finding: Piecemeal exclusion worked best in group theory, so HRL is not tuned only to number theory where it was built. Giving some but not all agents counterexample-barring seemed to improve the modifications. Example in number theory: 'a*a*a = a' was repaired by excluding a = 1 (the same case that monster-barring would bar).
numbers: Counts of good modifications were too low to fix optimal parameters (author's statement).
limits: Preliminary, few modifications per setting. No statistics.
agent_relevance: Mixing repair styles across parallel attempts (some may exclude, some may not) is a candidate diversity lever, but it is untested beyond this toy.

source: Pease (2007) thesis, chapter 12; Colton and Pease (2004) Theorem Modifier (TM)
finding: The one test of Lakatos-style repair with an automatic check. TM takes a false or open algebra conjecture, uses a model finder to get supporting and falsifying examples, lets HR invent a restricting concept, and keeps only modified claims that the prover Otter proves. Outputs are classed as probably uninteresting if only the trivial algebra satisfies the condition or if the condition just restates the claim.
numbers: 98 invented non-theorems from TPTP (made by removing axioms, changing quantifiers, altering variables, brackets): valid modifications for 83 percent, average 3.1 modifications each. 9 real TPTP non-theorems: 7 modified (78 percent). Otter and MACE 10 s, HR 3000 steps.
quote: From 98 invented non-theorems, TM produced valid modifications for 83% of them
limits: Validity means a proof exists, not that the claim is useful. No baseline such as random condition addition. Many repairs may be trivial (the thesis flags this by its own filter). Invented non-theorems are synthetic mutations.
agent_relevance: Best template for a code-checked repair loop: counterexamples and supporters from a checker, a restricting condition, then re-check by a prover. The 'trivial or restates the claim' filter is a needed guard against vacuous repair. Link: lemma discovery and conjecturing subfield.

source: Pease (2007) thesis, chapter 11 (philosophical evaluation) and abstract
finding: The thesis judges its model against criteria from Thagard, Sloman, Popper and Lakatos, centring on consilience (how many conjectures a theory accounts for) and simplicity. This is argument, not experiment. It sets the methods out as computable procedures: surrender, monster-barring, exception-barring (piecemeal exclusion, strategic withdrawal), lemma-incorporation.
numbers: No numerical test. Method of lemma-incorporation and proof-generated concepts are described but not measured with the system.
limits: Philosophical fit is not performance evidence.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean operator list to compare with SCHEMA O1-O8. Repair types map onto S5 REVISE choices, but the mapping is design, not evidence (status [D]).

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: When the loop is told the correct label (oracle), self-correction raises accuracy. When it has no oracle, accuracy stays flat or falls. Most gains in earlier papers came from the oracle that stops the loop when the answer is right.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 standard, oracle self-correct 84.3 (per Table 2 layout), intrinsic round 1 75.1 and round 2 74.7. CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) and 41.8 (round 2). GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 and 80.0. HotpotQA GPT-3.5 26.0 to 25.0 (100 questions). Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0 to 43.5 and 36.5.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Reasoning tasks only; some models and prompts; the oracle table row order in the PDF text is partly scrambled so oracle numbers should be rechecked before citing. Does not test external tools.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2 and G3: a repair loop must be driven by a real failing output, never by the model's own doubt. Any Lakatos loop with a model-judged 'counterexample' will inherit this failure.

source: Huang et al. (2024) same paper: why accuracy drops, and debate vs voting
finding: On GSM8K, GPT-3.5 keeps its first answer 74.7 percent of the time after two rounds. Among changes, correct-to-wrong is more frequent than wrong-to-correct. Different feedback prompts did not rescue it. Multi-agent debate does not beat self-consistency at equal response count.
numbers: Self-consistency at 9 responses about 88 percent vs debate at 9 responses about 83 percent on GSM8K (GPT-3.5, full test set). Debate at 3 responses only slightly above self-consistency at 3 (about 83 vs 82.5; table text partly scrambled). Feedback-prompt variants on GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K ranged 88.0 to 91.0 vs 91.5 baseline.
limits: Models of 2023. Table 7 layout scrambled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: Reconfirms G9 (no debate) and G4. Counterexample hunting by a second model persona is a debate in disguise and should be avoided; use code.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (BIG-Bench Mistake)
finding: Split the problem in two. Finding the wrong step is hard for all tested models. Fixing the step when told where it is works well. The bottleneck of self-repair is locating the fault, not repairing it.
numbers: 300 chain-of-thought traces (255 wrong, 45 right) over 5 tasks. Best model GPT-4 reaches 52.87 overall mistake-finding accuracy with direct step prompting. Backtracking with true mistake location, word sorting: wrong traces fixed +23.53 points while 11.11 points of right traces broken. With random location: +11.76 fixed, 15.56 broken. A small trained mistake classifier helps once accuracy is about 60-70 percent.
limits: Few right traces (45 per task set) so loss estimates are noisy. Authors note net gain depends on base accuracy: 50 percent base becomes 68.6, 99 percent base becomes 92.8.
agent_relevance: This is the Lakatos point in numbers: a global failure is not a located failure. Our code must locate which premise or step a counterexample hits (SUBFIELDS question a); once located, a model can repair. Random location still beats nothing but breaks many correct traces.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction
finding: Three claims after reviewing many papers. (1) No prior work shows self-correction with feedback from a prompted model, except on tasks unusually suited to it. (2) Self-correction works where reliable external feedback exists. (3) Large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Many positive results used unfair baselines or an oracle that decides when to stop.
numbers: Survey, no single effect size.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Survey; the quote is paraphrased from the abstract's item (1) and the exception clause matters.
agent_relevance: Backs the rule: the checker, not the model, supplies the counterexample. Gives a checklist item for our own test: report whether the stop signal used ground truth.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: A retry loop that writes a verbal reflection after each failed attempt, using real execution signals, raises pass rates. Reflexion is the closest LLM analogue to proof-and-refutation cycles, with unit tests acting as counterexamples.
numbers: HumanEval Python pass@1 91.0 vs 80.1 for GPT-4 baseline. MBPP Python 77.0 vs 80.0 (worse than baseline, as reported). HumanEval Rust 68 vs 60. MBPP Rust 75 vs 71. LeetcodeHard Python 15.0 vs 7.5. HotPotQA about +20 points. Ablation: reflection gave an 8 percent absolute boost over episodic memory alone on 100 HotPotQA questions. Test suite capped at 6 self-written unit tests.
quote: 91% pass@1 accuracy on the HumanEval coding benchmark
limits: Stop signal is the model's own generated tests; for HotPotQA a ground-truth correctness bit is used. Small samples (100 questions).
agent_relevance: Shows the loop works when the check is real. The MBPP regression (next line) shows what happens when the check is incomplete.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: false-positive analysis on MBPP Python
finding: Reflexion lost to the baseline on MBPP Python because self-written tests passed wrong programs. The loop stopped at a false pass. False negatives are harmless (the agent can reflect and try again) but false positives end the search on a wrong answer.
numbers: MBPP Python false-positive rate 16.3 percent vs 1.4 percent on HumanEval Python. Baselines were similar (80 vs 82 percent). True-positive/false-negative rates for HumanEval Python 0.99/0.40; MBPP Python 0.84/0.59.
quote: false negatives are preferred over false positives
limits: One model (GPT-4), one test-writing prompt.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G3: a pass is only a pass against tests the answer was not fitted to. For a Lakatos loop, a weak counterexample generator (few tests) silently lowers accuracy; the stopping rule should demand independent held-out probes.

source: Chen et al. (2024, ICLR) Teaching large language models to self-debug
finding: Repair with execution feedback beats repair from explanation alone. One debugging turn gets most of the gain. Debugging a greedy program matched or beat sampling many programs (sample efficiency).
numbers: MBPP (Codex): baseline 61.4, with unit-test feedback 69.8, +trace 70.8. GPT-4: 72.8 to 80.4 (unit tests). TransCoder GPT-4 77.3 to 90.4. Without any execution, MBPP GPT-4 72.8 to 76.4 (+3.6), TransCoder Codex up to +5. Spider: greedy + debug matched 16 samples and 8 samples + debug beat 32 samples. Accuracy gain after the first turn within 0.1 percent.
limits: Only part of the unit tests shown in the prompt; rest held out for evaluation, so the gains hold on unseen tests. Codex, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, StarCoder only.
agent_relevance: Evidence that repair can beat resampling when the check gives concrete runtime output. Cap repair at about one to two turns. The hidden-test split is the right template for G3.

source: Olausson et al. (2024, ICLR) Is self-repair a silver bullet for code generation?
finding: At equal sampling cost, repair often does not beat drawing fresh independent samples. It helps only when most of the budget goes to diverse first drafts and when the feedback is good. Feedback quality, not repair skill, is the limit.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 first samples plus 1 repair each (up to 20 samples) gives 1.05 times the pass rate of pass@20; 2 first samples plus 10 repairs each (22 samples) gives 0.97 times pass@22. Replacing GPT-4's own explanations with a human programmer's raised the fraction of repaired programs that pass from 33.3 to 52.6 percent (1.58 times). Stronger-model feedback beat the baseline at all budgets.
quote: Self-repair is not a silver bullet
limits: HumanEval and APPS, Python; 3 models (Code Llama 13B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4). Authors give only conjectures on why repair and generation rates move together.
agent_relevance: The key control for SUBFIELDS question (c): compare repair vs resampling at equal tokens. Expect repair to lose on easy items and win mainly when the counterexample message is informative. Supports G12.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback
finding: Generic self-feedback helps style and preference tasks but not math. Specific, actionable feedback matters. For math the model says 'everything looks good' almost always, so no repair happens.
numbers: Average gain about 20 points over one-step generation on the paper's tasks (mostly preference tasks). Math Reasoning: base 64.1 vs Self-Refine 64.1 (0 gain) for GPT-3.5; GPT-4 92.9 to 93.1; with an oracle that flags wrong answers 64.06 to 68.9. ChatGPT feedback said 'everything looks good' in 94 percent of math cases. Code optimization 27.5 (specific feedback) vs 26.0 (generic) vs 24.8 (none). Sentiment transfer 43.2 vs 31.2 with generic feedback. Failure types in a sample: ignores feedback 25 percent, introduces a new problem 20 percent, not robust 10 percent.
limits: Many tasks are judged by a model or by preference, which is the self-preference bias the schema warns about (G5).
agent_relevance: Where there is no executable check, expect no gain. Where feedback is specific and located, it pays. Repair can introduce new faults 20 percent of the time, so every repair must be re-tested on the old counterexamples (regression set).

source: Gou et al. (2024, ICLR) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
finding: The same critique loop with no tool gives little or no gain; with search or a code interpreter it gives clear gains. The ablation isolates the tool as the active ingredient.
numbers: Text-Davinci-003, free-form QA exact match (AmbigNQ / TriviaQA / HotpotQA): CoT 44.2 / 67.4 / 33.7; CRITIC without tool 42.0 / 67.3 / 34.9; CRITIC with tool 50.0 / 72.7 / 38.7; oracle variant 59.8 / 77.0 / 43.1. Abstract: ChatGPT +7.7 F1 over 3 QA tasks, +7.0 percent absolute on 3 math tasks.
limits: Oracle setting corrects only known-wrong answers, so it is an upper bound, not a deployable result.
agent_relevance: Same message as Tyen and Huang: an outside check beats self-critique. In a Lakatos loop the counterexample finder must be a program, a search, or a held-out test, not a prompt.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training language models to self-correct via reinforcement learning (SCoRe)
finding: Prompting and supervised fine-tuning make self-correction worse or zero. Two-stage multi-turn reinforcement learning makes it positive. Spending a budget on one correction round per parallel sample beats all parallel samples. A fix to the structural problem: the model learns to leave a correct first answer alone.
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Flash on MATH: base model turn 1 52.6, turn 2 41.4 (-11.2); STaR 55.4 to 41.2 (-14.2); Pair-SFT 52.4 to 54.2 (+1.8); SCoRe 60.0 to 64.4 (+4.4). Abstract: +15.6 points on MATH and +9.1 on HumanEval over base self-correction. Base model: 15.8 percent of correct answers turned wrong. At 32-solution budget, parallel gives +7.4, mix of parallel and one self-correction round gives +10.5.
limits: Requires training; Google models only. Gain figures are for intrinsic correction on tasks with a simple correct-or-not reward.
agent_relevance: Our agent cannot train, so only the scaffold side applies: keep the first answer unless a located failure exists (G1, G2) and use sequential repair on top of parallel samples, not instead of them.

source: Qiu et al. (2024, ICLR) Phenomenal yet puzzling: inductive reasoning with hypothesis refinement
finding: Propose-select-refine loops work when a symbolic interpreter filters the rules. Without that, refinement does not help. The loop is the closest published LLM test of conjecture-and-refutation on rule induction.
numbers: ACRE raw accuracy: direct prompting 64.0, self-consistency N=5 65.0, self-refine (LM as own interpreter) 70.0, hypothesis refinement T=1,N=1 78.2, T=3,N=1 77.8, T=3,N=5 82.5. ACRE task accuracy 28.0 direct vs 59.0 for T=3,N=5. MiniSCAN task accuracy 0.0 for direct and T=1 vs 46.0 at T=3,N=1. MiniARC: refinement 18.7 raw vs 33.1 direct (worse).
limits: Synthetic symbolic tasks (ACRE, MiniSCAN, List Functions, MiniARC); some rows of the table text are scrambled so only the ACRE and MiniSCAN rows are cited. Not compared at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: On rule-induction items a refine loop with a code interpreter beats direct and voting, except on pattern-matching grids where direct prompting wins. This is the best evidence for a counterexample-driven loop on our ARC-style items (SUBFIELDS question c), with the caveat on MiniARC.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: rule application gap and how LMs refine
finding: Models propose rules they cannot apply. When the same model acts as interpreter, accuracy collapses. During refinement they mostly add an exception for the one failing example instead of rethinking the rule, which is exception-barring in Lakatos's terms. This fails when the first rule is wholly wrong.
numbers: MiniSCAN task accuracy drops from above 80 percent with a symbolic interpreter to near zero with the LM as interpreter. ACRE task accuracy 59.0 symbolic vs 47.0 (approx, from figure) with LM. Example refinement: 'Remove the value 2' became 'Remove the value 6 if present. If not, remove the value 2'.
quote: adding exceptions for a specific example, rather than starting from entirely new hypotheses
limits: Figure values partly read from a scrambled figure; text claims are reliable.
agent_relevance: Predicts the failure mode of a Lakatos loop: patching with ad hoc exceptions (what Lakatos called degenerating). Add a code rule that counts patches and forces a restart or new representation when exceptions pile up (links to Anytime search and restarts).

source: Wang et al. (2024, ICLR) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models
finding: On ARC, going through explicit natural-language hypotheses then Python programs checked on the training examples improves accuracy. Human choice among model hypotheses gives only a little more, so the bottleneck is hypothesis generation, not program writing.
numbers: 100 random ARC tasks, GPT-4: direct prompting 17, program only 23, LLM-summarised hypotheses 30, human-selected hypotheses 33, human-written hypotheses 45. Human selection: of 49 tasks with a usable hypothesis among 64, 33 (67 percent) gave correct programs. DSL search system Icecuber 43. Without a program step, accuracy fell to 19.
limits: One 100-task sample; GPT-4 of 2023; feedback is up to 3 rounds of execution. Low false-positive rate reported for passing programs, so G3 risk is smaller here.
agent_relevance: Gives the equal-footing numbers for a verify-by-execution hypothesis loop on ARC. The gap from 33 to 45 shows hypothesis proposal is the limiting step, which a refutation loop alone does not fix.

source: Li et al. (2025, ICML) One example shown, many concepts known: CounterMATH
finding: Benchmark of university-level statements where the right move is a counterexample. Most open models are poor at it, and drill-based training on school math does not help. Reasoning models use many tokens without proportional gain.
numbers: 1,216 statement-rationale pairs, about 88 percent true and 12 percent false (macro F1 used). Open 7B models score about 28-37 F1; Qwen2.5-Math-72B 41.8; DeepSeek-R1 80.7. MetaMath and rho-math produce counterexamples in only 26.5 and 18.3 percent of cases. Hard fields: topology and real analysis. Fine-tune on 1,025 samples lifts Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct F1 from about 38-39 to 41.1 (table text scrambled). Out-of-distribution: MATH 80.5 to 87.9 and AIME 2024 20.0 to 30.0 for the fine-tuned 7B (row order from text, treat as indicative).
limits: Judging of example quality uses a model-based matcher (97 percent and 93.5 percent agreement with humans in checks). Gain from SFT is small on the in-domain metric.
agent_relevance: Finding a counterexample is a separate skill from checking a claim, and it is weak in small models. Our code should supply counterexample search (enumeration, mutation) and not rely on the model to invent them.

source: Li et al. (2026, rejected from ICLR 2026) Learning to disprove: formal counterexample generation with LLMs
finding: Fine-tuning on counterexample tasks made by symbolic mutation of theorems (drop a hypothesis, then ask for a counterexample with a Lean proof that it works) strongly beats existing provers on this task. Lean checks every claim, so there is no judge noise.
numbers: Validation set pass@1: fine-tuned model 49.8 percent vs 25.4 (Leanabell), 23.7 (STP), 9.8 (Kimina-distill), 14.0 (Goedel-v2), 14.1 (DeepSeek-v2); pass@9 54.1 vs best baseline 39.9. Abstract states relative gains of 47 to 74 percent in pass@1 over the strongest baseline on three new benchmarks.
limits: Paper was rejected at ICLR 2026 (marked on the PDF), self-built benchmarks, trained models; baselines are theorem provers not built for disproving.
agent_relevance: The mutation idea fits our code side: generate (claim, dropped premise) pairs and classify counterexamples by which premise they violate. This directly matches Lakatos's local vs global counterexample test (SUBFIELDS question a).

source: Synthesis across b07, b09, b13, b14, b16 (feedback source versus gain)
finding: Across studies the same split appears. Executable or external feedback gives gains; self-judged feedback gives zero or negative; located feedback beats unlocated. Rank by gain: human explanation (33.3 to 52.6 percent repaired) > unit test output (Codex MBPP +8.4) > model-only (+3.6 GPT-4 MBPP) > intrinsic reasoning (negative).
numbers: Codex MBPP 61.4 to 69.8 with unit tests vs 61.4 to 66.2 best model-only; GPT-4 MBPP 72.8 to 80.4 vs 76.4; Huang GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 intrinsic. Cross-paper comparison only, models and tasks differ.
limits: Not a controlled comparison; assembled from the lines above.
agent_relevance: Design rule: invest in the counterexample producer (code, tests, mutation) before the repair prompt. The repair prompt is the cheap part.

source: Competing explanations for why self-repair underperforms (Olausson 2024; Tyen 2024; Huang 2024; Kumar 2024)
finding: Four rival accounts. (1) Fault locating is the bottleneck (Tyen, with oracle location fixing +23.5 points on wrong traces). (2) Feedback quality is the bottleneck (Olausson, human vs model feedback 52.6 vs 33.3 percent). (3) Models cannot judge their own correctness, so they flip right answers (Huang, Kumar: 15.8 percent of correct answers turned wrong). (4) Distribution mismatch in training, fixed by on-policy RL (Kumar). The first three are compatible; the fourth needs training.
numbers: See the four source lines. No study isolates all four in one experiment.
limits: Interpretive synthesis. No single paper tests which factor dominates.
agent_relevance: One experiment would discriminate: hold repair prompt fixed, vary (a) located vs unlocated fault, (b) code vs model feedback, at equal tokens. This is the test to run for question (c).

source: Pease (2007) thesis: what the evaluation leaves open, and absence of LLM replications
finding: No source found in this session that runs a Lakatos-labelled LLM loop (monster-barring, lemma-incorporation, concept refinement) with a matched resampling control. LLM work measures the pieces (counterexample search, located repair, exception patching) without the Lakatos taxonomy. The thesis itself lacks controls and sample sizes.
numbers: Web searches for LLM plus Lakatos plus counterexample returned only CounterMATH, Learning to Disprove and generic generate-verify-correct descriptions. Not exhaustive.
limits: Absence of evidence in a limited search. Search engine coverage is partial.
agent_relevance: Treat the three-way counterexample taxonomy as an untested design [D], not an established mechanism. The first deliverable should be a small test set with known counterexamples and an equal-token comparison.
